The Saudi mortgage market grew in Q3. The average Saudi mortgage did not.

SAMA's Q3 numbers: banks signed 29,111 new residential mortgage contracts with individuals, up 18.6% from 24,535 a year earlier. The value of that lending fell 4.6% to SAR 17.27 billion. Put those two together and the average new loan has shrunk by about a fifth year on year, to roughly SAR 593,000.

The mix explains most of it. Villa contracts fell 3.3% to 11,170 even as total contracts rose 18.6%, so the growth came from apartments and smaller tickets. At finance companies the same rotation is clearer: apartment financing reached SAR 310 million in Q3 against SAR 210 million for villas. GASTAT's Q3 price index points the same way - villas down 7.7% year on year, apartments up 1.7%, residential land up 4.9%.

My read: this is not a weaker buyer, it is a different one. Demand is moving down the ticket size, and the villa is losing price and financing volume at the same time. For anyone underwriting residential today, unit mix is becoming a bigger lever on returns than headline sales price - a feasibility built on villa absorption from two years ago is modelling a buyer who is no longer there.

Is your residential mix moving toward apartments, or are you waiting for villas to find a floor?

#SaudiArabia #RealEstate #Riyadh #Vision2030 #RealEstateFinance
cards.why: Real estate investment and market data analysis in Saudi Arabia.

options.text: That drop in average loan size to SAR 593,000 means a higher volume of smaller inquiries. Are brokerages actually staffing up to handle that volume?

That shift toward apartments and a SAR 593,000 average loan size means a much higher volume of incoming leads. In the speed-to-lead systems I build, handling that jump without letting enquiries sit is where deals are actually won now.
Honestly I'd look at it the other way around. Waiting for villas to find a floor misses the point if the actual buyer pool has permanently moved down to that SAR 593,000 average ticket size.

cards.post_text:
The Right Property for One Investor Can Be the Wrong One for Another.

Two investors can examine the same property, agree on its location and recognise its potential, yet reach completely different conclusions.

That does not necessarily mean one of them is wrong.

Their objectives may simply be different.

One investor may prioritise rental income. Another may be focused on long term value. A third may need greater flexibility because their capital could be required elsewhere.

Each objective changes how the opportunity should be evaluated.

The expected holding period matters. So does the amount of capital committed, the investor’s tolerance for uncertainty and the ability to manage an investment if circumstances change.

This is why I believe property selection should never begin with a list of attractive developments alone.

It should begin with understanding the investor.

Only then can the property be assessed against the criteria that actually matter.

In Dubai, the range of available developments can make the search itself feel like progress. But more options do not automatically lead to better decisions.

Clarity about your objectives helps narrow the field and makes comparisons more meaningful.

The question is not simply whether a property is attractive. It is whether it is appropriate for the person committing the capital.

#DubaiRealEstate #InvestmentStrategy #CapitalAllocation #KhoudarTheKey

Before you spend more on AI, look at how your team works
If your team takes two days to send a quote, where do those two days go? Is someone looking up prices, writing the quote or waiting for a manager to approve it? Each answer points to a different fix.
That’s what stood out to me in the research behind From Set Up to Set for Growth, the SME playbook from du and Huawei UAE. Of the 648 businesses interviewed across all seven emirates, 63% used productivity and collaboration tools, while only 8% reached what du classifies as advanced digital maturity. Setup costs and skills gaps were the two most cited barriers, at 47% and 45%. du’s research announcement
The playbook looks at how businesses can get more from the tools they already use, from serving customers and improving productivity to managing cash flow and keeping operations running. When data is missing, the model fills the gap.

I recently read a special dossier asking whether history can survive AI. 

Historians, it turns out, face the same problem  in healthcare: the model is only as good as the evidence it can see.

Historian Frédéric Clavert puts it simply. We have few sources on Khafre, more on Louis XIV, and an enormous amount on any twentieth-century leader. 

AI models inherit that imbalance.

Asked about a poorly documented episode, a model may not say "I don’t know". It may produce a plausible story, sometimes an entire fabricated massacre, modelled on a real one.

The numbers are humbling. On HistBench, a benchmark of 414 questions written by historians, GPT-4o scored 18.6%. These are not obscure questions, they test the ability to reason with incomplete, contested and contextual evidence, exactly what history demands.

The wider constraint is data itself. 

Epoch AI estimates that the effective stock of quality, public human-generated text could be fully used for model training sometime between 2026 and 2032, depending on how aggressively developers scale. 

After that, models will increasingly learn from synthetic data, private archives and other models’ outputs. Rare, ambiguous or poorly documented cases risk being drowned out by the well-documented majority.

Medicine knows this story.

Most genomic reference data still comes disproportionately from people of European ancestry. 

A patient in Riyadh may therefore be, statistically, a rare
cards.why: Thoughtful post on medical AI data gaps and intake forms. Perfect match for discovery and intake audit.

options.text: "A confident version of the gap" is spot on, Nabila. If the intake form misses a structured variable upfront, no prompt downstream recovers it.

That point about forcing the AI to declare what it can't establish is everything. When I built a voice agent at a hackathon, we moved the logic out of the prompt and into tested TypeScript. The model could phrase the response, but deterministic code enforced what was factual so it couldn't invent rules when data was missing.

Starting the AI strategy at the intake form is the right framing, Nabila. In practice, how are you seeing clinics handle the tension between capturing structured data and keeping intake simple enough that staff or patients actually fill it out correctly?

The Saudi dental market does not behave like most others.

In many markets, a single-specialty practice can thrive on referrals: orthodontics only, endodontics only. In Saudi Arabia, patients generally prefer one place for everything: hygiene, restorative, endodontics, orthodontics, implants, cosmetic and paediatric care. They do not want to repeat their history at three different clinics.

That is why clinics here tend to be larger and multi-specialty. It changes the economics:
- Larger footprint, higher rent
- More specialties, more doctors and contracts
- More equipment, higher capital outlay

In return, patients stay for years and each specialty feeds the others.

You will not have the strongest name in every specialty under one roof. The smarter approach is to choose the core specialties your reputation will rest on, and support the rest with competent clinicians and a clear internal referral system.

Workforce availability has improved. There are more Saudi and non-Saudi dentists, general and specialist, than a decade ago. Non-Saudi and contract clinicians can be valuable for scarce specialties or peak hours.

Saudization in dentistry is now operational. The second phase started in January 2026 at 55% for private facilities with three or more dental professionals, with a minimum registered salary of SAR 9,000 for a Saudi dentist to count. Team mix and salary structure belong in your financial model from day one, not after hiring.

options.text: That line about the first call being part of the product hits home. When multi-specialty patients call in, do your receptionists route them by doctor or by severity?

That point about the first call being part of the product is where edge cases show up fast. In the bilingual voice receptionists I build, callers mixing Arabic and English on phone lines drop off if the confirmation step isn't tight. Getting that initial intake right is what keeps the cross-referrals to other specialties alive.

Choosing core specialties for your reputation makes complete sense, Dr. Saleh. But when supporting specialties rely on internal referrals, how do you handle clinician incentives? If a doctor is paid a percentage of production, they can be hesitant to pass a patient over to an internal colleague.

Today I attended the 4th Edition of ONE BROKER GROUP aka OBG Connect, and I walked away with some valuable insights, fresh perspectives and, of course, a few new connections!

The buyers haven't disappeared. Their confidence to commit has changed. Cherif Sleiman from Property Finder shared some fascinating data about buyer behaviour. People are still searching. They're still enquiring. They're still exploring opportunities.

But there's a gap between what sellers believe their properties are worth and what buyers are currently prepared to pay. And THAT is where the real conversation begins!

We also heard from Ben Bandari and Umar Bin Farooq about why the UAE continues to attract international interest.

Safety. Lifestyle. Opportunity. Vision. Growth.

But my biggest takeaway wasn't about statistics... It was about RESPONSIBILITY.

As real estate professionals, we need to stop confusing activity with opportunity. Just because someone enquires doesn't mean they're ready to buy... Just because someone wants to sell doesn't mean their asking price reflects the market. And just because a deal CAN happen doesn't mean it SHOULD happen.

Sometimes our most valuable advice is simply: "Let's look at the facts before making a decision."

At Chas Everitt Dubai, that's the kind of business I want us to build... Not pressure. Not empty promises. Not chasing commissions at the expense of relationships. Just honest conversations, market knowledge and people who trust us enough to come back.
cards.why: GM of Dubai real estate brokerage discussing lead quality and broker activity vs opportunity.

options.text: Spotting the difference between an enquiry and a real opportunity early is key, Janine. How are your brokers filtering those initial touchpoints right now?

That distinction between buyer search volume and readiness to commit is key. A lot of that friction comes from treating every initial web form like an urgent deal instead of asking two qualifying questions up front.

I'd push back slightly on the idea of a slower market. The enquiry volume is usually still there when confidence shifts, but brokers get bogged down chasing lead activity instead of setting clear criteria on day one.

I Went From IT Leadership to Real Estate Relationship Management in Dubai. What I Discovered Changed My Perspective.

People might wonder:

Why would someone with a background in Senior IT Management move into Relationship Management in Dubai's real estate industry?

My answer is simple:

I wanted to understand business from another perspective — not only from behind the technology, but also from the customer-facing side.

And what I discovered was fascinating.

After years of managing IT infrastructure, operations, cybersecurity, enterprise systems and technical teams, I started looking at real estate businesses through a different lens.

I noticed something that deserves more attention across the industry:

Some real estate companies invest heavily in marketing, sales teams and impressive projects, but their technology and IT processes don't always support the business effectively.

Here are some challenges that I believe deserve serious attention:

🔴 1. CRM systems that don't deliver their full value

Companies invest in CRM platforms, but lead assignment, follow-up, customer history and reporting can remain fragmented.

🔴 2. Disconnected systems

Sales, marketing, finance, customer service and property management sometimes operate in separate systems without proper integration.

🔴 3. Too much manual work

Processes that could be automated still depend on emails, spreadsheets, WhatsApp messages and manual approvals.

🔴 4. Poor IT reporting and visibility

Management needs

options.text: The point about WhatsApp and spreadsheets taking over from the CRM hits closest to home, Sarwar. Are agents in Dubai usually keeping client histories in their personal chats?

Off-plan Dubai or a ready home? They're not the same buy.

Off-plan usually means a lower entry cost and payments tied to construction milestones, but a longer wait before you can move in or collect rent. You're buying from plans, so layout, light and finish are still on paper.

A ready home lets you walk the finished unit, check the workmanship, and often move in or let it soon after transfer. You pay closer to full price up front, but construction and handover risk are mostly behind you.

In Q3 2026, off-plan made up 69% of Dubai residential sales (Richmond Properties' analysis of Dubai Land Department data). Popular doesn't mean right for your timeline.

Off-plan tends to suit longer horizons. Ready suits end users who need to move in, or investors who want rent now. The full side-by-side is in the carousel, with details in the comments.

Which way are you leaning, off-plan or ready? Comment below or DM me.

#OffPlanDubai #DubaiProperty #AbuDhabiRealEstate #UAERealEstate

cards.author_headline: Healthcare Marketing Strategist | Prosthodontist helping practice owners fill chairs without adding staff | Marketing, front desk, AI & recall run as one system | Host, The Dental Lens Podcast | Founder, Techiedentist |
cards.post_text:
Your team is probably already using AI.

The question is whether they know what never goes into it.

A front desk coordinator pastes a patient's message into a free chatbot to "make the reply sound nicer."
A dentist uploads a clinical note to summarise it faster.
Nobody thinks they're breaking a rule, because there isn't one.

That's the real risk in most practices. Not the tool you buy. The tools your team already uses, on personal phones, with no written policy.

A one-page AI Use Policy fixes more than most software will:

→ What AI is allowed to be used for
→ What never goes into a chatbot
→ A 60-second de-identification check before anything is pasted
→ A signature from every person on the team

And the policy only works if the basics behind it are in place: signed agreements with every tool that touches patient information (a BAA in the US, a data processing agreement in the UK and Canada), and a clear answer to "which AI tools is my team already using?"

I covered how to check all of that in this week's Lessons from the Lens, and the one-page AI Use Policy your clinic must have.

If I walked into your practice tomorrow and asked your newest team member what never goes into a chatbot, what would they say?

#DentalPractice #DentalAI #PatientPrivacy #PracticeManagement
cards.why: Peer vendor discussing clinic AI use policies. Direct overlap with deterministic code vs prompt opinions.

options.text: A one-page policy is a great start, but if staff are resorting to free chatbots to rephrase patient messages, it usually means their own system is just too slow to draft replies.

When I built a voice agent at a hackathon, we kept privacy rules in tested code so the model couldn't even touch restricted inputs. A written policy gives legal cover, but when a clinic is packed at 4 PM, hard software guardrails are what actually stop patient data from slipping through.

Asking the newest team member what never goes into a chatbot is a great test. But if you asked them *why* they used it, do you think it's mostly to rephrase patient messages or summarise clinical notes? Knowing which specific task is driving them to unapproved tools changes how you fix it.

How would you know a support portal is saving money?

Record three numbers before launch:
- Tickets per week
- Cost per ticket
- How often a customer has to contact you twice for the same problem

Measure again after three months. 

Gartner's 2019 research found only 9% of customers fully resolved their issues through self-service, so track what actually gets solved, not just what gets redirected.

This applies across  Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and USA.

Which of the three numbers could you pull today?

#AIGovernance #Measurement
cards.why: AI agency CEO talking support metrics and ticket costs. Good peer discussion on measurement.

options.text: That third one about repeat contacts is the hardest to actually pull. Do most teams have a way to link a second call back to the first ticket, or does it usually live in someone's head?

Tracking how often a customer has to contact you twice tells you more than ticket volume ever will. When coordination lives across phone calls and WhatsApp instead of a ticket system, repeat contacts are where the real volume hides.

The piece that usually gets missed is that tickets per week only counts what actually gets logged. If people are messaging instead of using the portal, the real volume is sitting somewhere else entirely.

cards.post_text:
The best proposal I ever sent was one page long.

In Dubai we were pitching a real estate brokerage. Twelve agents, a founder who still answered every lead himself, and two other agencies in the running. One of them was much bigger than us. I found out later their deck was 34 pages.

On the call the founder talked for almost 40 minutes. Leads going cold over the weekend. Agents posting whatever they wanted on Instagram. A launch in March he was nervous about. A budget he mentioned twice, so I knew it was real.

After the call I didn't open our proposal template.

I wrote one page. His three problems, in his words. What we'd do about each one. The price he'd mentioned. A start date two weeks before his launch.

He signed the next morning. On the kickoff call he said: "You were the only ones who sent back what I actually said."

The other agencies weren't worse than us. Their proposals were about them. Case studies, team photos, process diagrams. Ours was about him.

Most proposals are long because they're written from a template, not from the call.

The client already told you what to put in it. Your job is to hand it back to them, clearly, while they still remember saying it.

What's the shortest proposal you've ever closed with?
cards.why: Dubai agency founder discussing fast proposals and founder-led lead handling. Excellent fit.

options.text: "You were the only ones who sent back what I actually said" is the best compliment a proposal can get. Did you keep that one page as your base template after that?
"Leads going cold over the weekend" with twelve agents usually means the bottleneck is just getting to them fast enough. Did speed win the deal or was it the 1-page format?
Honestly the 34-page deck gets sent because templates are easier to write than listening to a 40-minute call. Writing what they actually said takes actual work.

We ran a holiday-home business in Dubai on group chats. Here’s what it actually cost us.

Not money, at first. Attention.

Every checkout clean was arranged in a WhatsApp group the evening before. Every photo of a finished apartment arrived in the same group, between voice notes and “ok”. Maintenance lived in another group. Owner questions in another.

What that cost:

→ Owner statements meant rebuilding the month from chats and Excel.
→ When something went wrong, nobody could say who did what, and when.

In three months our team handled 984 WhatsApp conversations and about 32,600 messages, with a median reply time of 1.6 minutes.

Replying was never the problem. Everything after the reply was.

So we built what we needed: one hub where every job, checklist, photo and invoice lives, set up by AI in about 15 minutes.

We open it free to service businesses in December.

If your business runs on group chats too, what does it cost you? I read every comment.

options.text: 32,600 messages in three months is a part-time job just reading the scroll. Did the breaking point come from missed cleans or owner statements?

Rebuilding a month from chat history and Excel is the exact moment coordination turns into a second job. In the outbound system I run for my own agency, keeping data out of the chat thread entirely was the only fix.
Replying in 1.6 minutes sounds fast, but if everything after the reply lives in WhatsApp, that speed doesn't actually save you time. Did you track how many hours went into chasing photo proof?

Dubai's property market is not stalling. It is settling into a more selective rhythm.

October home sales, at 9,999 transactions worth AED 21.27 billion, held almost level with September, even as they remained well below last year's peak. The median registered price was AED 1,650 per square foot, based on Dubai Land Department records analysed by Projectory.

The mix is shifting. Ready-home sales rose 13.8% in October, to 36.1% of transactions, as more buyers looked at completed stock. Off-plan still accounted for nearly two-thirds of sales, led by Dubai South and Jumeirah Village Circle.

Some 21.4% of Q3 tenancy transactions were agreed at a lower rent than the previous contract, up from 4.8% in the first quarter, according to Cavendish Maxwell. Average rents in September were still 5.5% higher than a year earlier, at AED 77.3 per square foot, but growth has slowed from 11.5% in September 2025. About 38,000 homes were handed over in the first nine months, up 41.4% on the same period last year.

My takeaway: after an exceptional run, advantage now sits with those who prepare carefully. Buyers and investors have more choice. Landlords who price to recent comparables will let faster. Sellers of quality, well-located homes still find demand. This is a healthier market, not a weaker one.

How are you reading the next six months?

#DubaiRealEstate #DubaiProperty #UAE #PropertyMarket #RealEstate

As a rule, Brits will go to extraordinary lengths to avoid an awkward conversation about money.

Barclays actually quantified this recently: half of UK adults consider talking about personal finances a taboo, and an estimated 2.8 million of us would rather “do anything” than talk about it.

Nowhere is that discomfort more visible than inside a dental surgery.

I spent years on both sides of the chair. First as a dentist diagnosing the problem and planning the care, then as an operator responsible for keeping the clinic running.

In all that time, I never met a clinician who enjoyed talking about prices. We spent five years studying anatomy, biomaterials, and clinical governance - so the moment treatment planning finishes, the instinct is to flee the room.

“Just ask reception for the printed estimate on your way out”. That was my default for my first year in practice.

But the front desk doesn't want that conversation either.

Standing at reception, within earshot of four other patients, asking someone if they’d like to apply for third-party finance through a clunky portal is deeply uncomfortable.

The patient nods politely, says they need to check with their partner, leaves the building, and the case quietly dies. Not because they didn't want the treatment, but because the conversation was embarrassing.

Private healthcare doesn't need a harder sell at the desk.

It needs a checkout that is discreet, flexible, and private on the patient’s own phone - while writing cleanly ba

That line about the case quietly dying outside the building because the conversation was embarrassing is so spot on. The drop-off happens in the exact gap between leaving the chair and opening a clunky portal later.
I'd argue the front desk doesn't just dislike the finance chat because it's awkward. They hate it because it blocks the queue when a phone call is ringing and three patients are waiting to check in.

Knowledge is the key to closing more deals.

Something I’ve learned over time, and something that has genuinely helped me close more deals, is that getting a lead doesn’t mean you’re going to close the deal.

The real work starts after you receive the inquiry.

Qualifying your client, understanding their business requirements, anticipating their concerns, and having answers to their questions are what make the difference.

Your client should feel that they don’t need to go back to Property Finder, Bayut, or another agent after viewing a property. They should feel confident that you’re the person who understands their requirements and can guide them through the entire process.

Especially in industrial real estate, knowing the property isn’t enough.

You should understand:

• Electricity load requirements and the process of power upgrades.
• Fit-out approvals and modification procedures.
• RTA, Dubai Municipality and other authority requirements.
• Zoning regulations and business licensing.
• RERA rules, regulations and tenants’ rights.
• Insurance requirements for the premises and the materials stored inside.
• Other business activities operating within a multi-tenant industrial compound.

These details might seem technical, but they can make or break a deal.

And here’s something I strongly believe in:

Never sell clients emotions. Sell them numbers, convenience, operational efficiency, ease of doing business and ROI.

Clients don’t just need someone to open warehouse doors

A delivery guarantee without customer obligations is an open-ended liability.

Carriers control dispatch readiness, vehicle availability and transit execution. They cannot control late customer loading, restricted receiving access or last-minute order changes. Yet unconditional service credits can make them pay for all three.

Effective contracts specify the promised milestone, required customer inputs, and which failures trigger credits, caps or exclusions. This may weaken the sales pitch, but it protects pricing discipline and preserves accountability.

A guarantee should cover controllable risk, not transfer every disruption to the carrier.

Where should carriers and customers draw the remedy boundary in Saudi transport contracts?

#TransportContracts #ServiceLevelAgreements #SaudiLogistics #FreightManagement #RiskAllocation
cards.why: Saudi logistics operations and risk allocation. Directly mirrors his medlog audit and workflow reliability domain.

options.text: Unconditional credits usually happen because carriers lack timestamped proof of when the truck hit the dock. Without that data, the client always wins the blame.

When I mapped a distributor's workflow, half the operational disputes came down to gate tracking. If dock arrival isn't logged automatically, late-loading penalties turn into endless WhatsApp arguments instead of clear contract remedies.
Putting required customer inputs in the contract is smart, but how are carriers in Saudi enforcing this on the ground when a key client refuses to acknowledge gate waiting times?

cards.post_text:
Dubai gives your next clinic 70% more rivals per resident than Abu Dhabi.

Choose the bigger city on clinic totals alone, and your second site can enter a far more crowded market than the spreadsheet suggests.

The Zavis UAE Open Healthcare Directory counted 2,337 clinics in Dubai and 1,241 in Abu Dhabi, using licensing data checked in March 2026.

The raw count makes Dubai look 88% larger. The population denominator changes the expansion decision.

Dubai reached 4.58 million residents at the end of 2025. Abu Dhabi reported 4,135,985 residents for 2024.

Put those official population figures under the licensing counts and Dubai has 5.1 clinics per 10,000 residents. Abu Dhabi has 3.0.

A clinic opening in Dubai therefore enters a market with about 70% more clinics competing for each resident.

Dental is even tighter. Dubai has about 0.95 dental clinics per 10,000 residents, compared with 0.34 in Abu Dhabi. That makes Dubai’s dental density nearly 2.8 times higher.

A second-site model built on clinic totals alone can make Dubai look roomier than it is.

The ratio measures supply density across each emirate. It cannot show whether those clinics share your specialty, catchment or payer mix. The population years also differ, so this comparison works as a market screen rather than a revenue forecast.

Before signing a lease, use the emirate-wide density to choose where to investigate. Then pull the district population, competing clinics within the target radius, rent, insurer pane
cards.why: AI clinic vendor analyzing UAE healthcare market density. Good opportunity to push back on density vs lead-waste math.

options.text: That 5.1 clinics per 10,000 residents in Dubai is steep, but high density usually masks an intake problem. How many of those 2,337 clinics actually answer their calls?

Comparing 0.95 dental clinics in Dubai to 0.34 in Abu Dhabi shows massive supply, but availability is where they fail. At 11 PM with severe tooth pain, I called 5 clinics: 3 didn't answer, 1 played a robotic hours voicemail, and 1 was Arabic-only. The 6th answered and got the booking.

That 70% higher density in Dubai makes the competition look intimidating on paper, but missed calls kill revenue long before market saturation does. Just 3 missed calls a day at a 30% booking rate and 1,000 SAR average value burns over 300,000 SAR a year. Fixing speed-to-lead matters way more than the neighbor count.

Most ConTech is built at a desk.  
Construction happens in the dust.

The foreman has gloves on.  
One bar of signal.  
Forty minutes before the crane leaves.

Your app needs six fields and a photo upload.

So he skips it. Or fills it in at 7 pm, relying on memory.

The dashboard shows green... The site tells a different story...

That's the gap between building technology for construction & building technology that actually works on a construction site.

I've seen this firsthand through our work at Emirates Contracting Company.

A process that works perfectly in an office doesn't necessarily work on site. The people using it, the conditions they work in & the time they have available all matter.

For ConTech founders, this is worth thinking about.

If using your product means adding steps to someone's already busy day, adoption will always be a challenge.

Build around the way people already work. Make capturing information easier, not another task to complete.

Build for the worst hour of the worst day... Not the best minute of the sales demo...

#ConTech #ConstructionTechnology #YogiGroup #Atinirmal #EmiratesContractingCompany #Dubai

options.text: The gloves-on and one bar of signal line hits the nail on the head. If field capture takes more than a single tap or quick voice note, it just turns into 7 PM guessing.

When I mapped a logistics operation with 23 drivers, we found this exact gap. The formal app required too much typing, so coordination defaulted to 50+ calls a day asking 'where are you?' If updating site status takes more than a few seconds, the dashboard ends up empty.

Designing for the worst hour on site is spot on, Atinirmal. When you look at how your site teams actually communicate in Dubai, is audio capture starting to replace forms, or are foremen still relying on WhatsApp group messages for real-time updates?

cards.author_headline: Founder, Emineva | Getting full-arch & full-mouth implant clinics in the UK and Australia recommended by ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI
cards.post_text:
Getting cited by AI isn't the same skill as ranking on Google. Most implant clinics optimise for the wrong one.

In our 515-clinic UK & AU study, 116 practices had 4.8+ stars and 300+ reviews. ChatGPT named zero of them.

Here's what actually decides whether ChatGPT names your clinic for £20k+ All-on-4 cases:

1. Crawler access: Can AI bots reach your site, or are they blocked in robots.txt?

2. Entity consistency: One name, address, and phone number written identically everywhere. Not "Harbour Implant Clinic" on your site and "Dr. Smith Dental" on Doctify.

3. Quotable facts: "All-on-4 runs £16,000 to £24,000 per arch and takes 3-6 months" is quotable. "We pride ourselves on excellence" is not.

4. Treatment depth: One dedicated page each for All-on-4, All-on-6, and Zygomatics. Not one paragraph covering everything.

5. Off-site consensus: Your site saying you're good is a claim. WhatClinic, Doctify, ClinicGo, and Reddit agreeing is a fact AI trusts.

6. Review specificity: "Great service" tells AI nothing. "Upper All-on-4 with Dr. Patel" tells it everything.

Six checks. Almost every clinic I audit fails at least four.

Nobody in dental marketing teaches this yet because they haven't noticed it's a different game. That's not a warning. That's the opening.







#ImplantDentistry #PrivateDentistry #DentalImplants #AllOn4 #FullArchRehabilitation #Prosthodontics #DentalPracticeManagement #DentalTourism #InternationalPatients #BusinessOfDentistry #TreatmentCoordinator #UKDenti
cards.why: Good breakdown of AI search optimization for dental implants, relevant audience.

options.text: That stat about 116 top-rated clinics getting zero ChatGPT citations is wild. Putting explicit numbers like £16k-£24k on the page gives the model something concrete to pull.

That point on review specificity makes a lot of sense. But even when AI names the clinic for a £20k All-on-4 case, getting recommended is only half the battle. If that high-intent enquiry sits in an inbox until the next morning, the citation gets wasted anyway.
Surprised to see Reddit in point 5 alongside Doctify. Are you finding ChatGPT weights anonymous forum comments just as heavily as verified patient review platforms for £20k procedures?

I look at 20 to 30 new off-plan deals a week, and AI now does most of the first pass. I still double check and decide, but it does the digging before I open a brochure.
 
Here's what it checks (in order):
 
- New launches, before they're on the DLD register.
- A score for 17 factors. 
- Comparables from registered DLD sales only, not asking prices.
- The payment plan against the buyer's cash, month by month to handover.
- The developer, location, plan and price, then a second AI checks the first one's work.
 
The comparables point matters more than people think. In the DLD export I work from, just over a quarter of the rows aren't sales at all - they're mortgages, gifts and registrations - so if you don't filter them out, the "market price" you're quoting is wrong before you start.
 
Same with developers. When I first rated them from portals and press releases, I had 2 of them exactly backwards. Awards and launch events tell you very little, what they've handed over and when tells you a lot.
 
But none of it replaces going to site. I'm still out every week, looking at progress, new sites, launches, briefings and keeping familiar with the UAE market.
 
If you're looking at off-plan and want a launch run through the same checks, message me.

options.text: Filtering out mortgages and gifts from the DLD export before the AI sees it makes a huge difference. Otherwise your baseline market price is skewed from the start.

I'd push back a bit on having a second AI check the first one's cashflow calculations. If the first model misreads a complex post-handover payment structure, the second prompt often accepts the context. Deterministic code handles month-by-month math much cleaner.

If you're a broker, this matters.

October's off-plan numbers have a clear winner.

Dubai recorded 11,937 property sales in October, and 7,660 of them were off-plan. That's 64% of the market.

One developer stood out. Binghatti registered 1,231 off-plan sales last month, about 16% of everything sold off-plan in the city. DAMAC was next with 773. Azizi, which leads the year so far, did 634.

That's almost double the number three.

Why it's selling, from what I see in the data:
→ Price point. Binghatti's median off-plan sale in October was about AED 1.25M. Three in four Dubai sales are apartments, and most of them trade around AED 1.1 to 1.2M.
→ New stock. Binghatti has launched 13 projects and almost 12,900 units this year, more units than any other developer.
→ Locations buyers already know, like Al Jaddaf and JVC.

And maybe that's what brokers should be focused on. What's actually selling right now, not what we'd like to sell.

This week I ran a market session with brokers built around these numbers. Three things from it worth sharing.

1. Lead with the data. "The market is slow" doesn't survive 11,937 sales in a month.

2. Answer developer trust with handover records, not adjectives. This year Emaar has handed over about 6,000 units, DAMAC about 3,500 and Binghatti about 2,250.

3. Every conversation ends with a date. Offer two options for the next meeting, never an open question.

Where to look first: Dubai South led off-plan sales with 713 deals in October, then JVC with

options.text: Ending every conversation with two date options makes a huge difference, Sambhav. Are your brokers locking those straight into a booking calendar on the call?

"Handover records, not adjectives" is the cleanest way to handle developer trust. At that AED 1.2M price point in places like JVC, buyers hear the same promises everywhere. Giving them exact delivery counts cuts through the noise immediately.

Data like 1,231 Binghatti sales in a month helps frame the pitch, but there's a practical gap. At that volume, buyers are usually messaging multiple agents for the same project simultaneously. If the initial response takes an hour, most buyers move on before you even get to offer two meeting dates.

cards.author_headline: Founder & CEO ADONIS Medical Group | Founder A.EggBank & Vitality Biotech | MD | IVF & Reproductive Tech | Global Egg Donor Bank | Life Sciences Investor | 25y Healthcare
cards.post_text:
When people talk about staff shortages in healthcare, they usually mean doctors and nurses 🔬

Recently I came across a survey of U.S. hospital CEOs by the American College of Healthcare Executives. After finances, staff shortages were their biggest concern. One detail stood out to me: almost three in four CEOs worry about a shortage of technicians, as many as worry about burnout among medical staff.

Technicians run the imaging rooms, laboratories and equipment that most treatment plans depend on. When a radiology or lab position stays empty, the effect shows up as longer waits for results, rescheduled scans and doctors making decisions with less information.

For a medical network, this changes how workforce planning looks. Training, career paths and recognition matter for technical staff as much as for physicians, because a diagnostic department works only as well as the people who operate it.

Which role in your organization would be hardest to replace tomorrow?

#healthcareleadership #healthcareworkforce #diagnostics #hospitalmanagement #ADONIS
cards.why: Medical group CEO discussing healthcare technician staff shortages.

options.text: That 3 in 4 CEO stat on technicians is eye-opening, Vitaliy. In your clinics, how much of the diagnostic delay is pure headcount versus techs bogged down by manual admin?

Rescheduled scans and delayed results hit the whole care chain hard. Often when a technical role feels understaffed, a chunk of their shift is getting eaten up by phone calls and manual log-chasing instead of running the machines. Clearing that extra admin work usually buys the existing team immediate capacity.

Focusing on technical career paths makes a lot of sense, Vitaliy. I'd only push back on treating this purely as a hiring shortage. When diagnostic coordination lives in manual handoffs and phone calls, it often looks like a staff shortage when it's really workflow friction. Adding headcount into a noisy process just duplicates the bottleneck.

Habibi, the UAE will humble your SaaS growth plan.

I spent five years at Xero, including founding the EMEA Hub team. Now I sit on the other side as a reseller in Dubai, watching overseas SaaS companies land here.

Most of them make the same 3 mistakes 👇

↳ Deals move on WhatsApp and coffee, not on sequences

2️⃣ 𝗚𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀
↳ SMEs here trust their accountant and their implementer more than your ads
↳ No partner programme means you’re invisible to them

3️⃣ 𝗜𝗴𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗹 𝗶𝘁’𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲
↳ If your product touches invoices, UAE e-invoicing is not optional
↳ Compliance and data questions come up in the first demo, not the tenth

The product usually isn’t the problem. 
The playbook is. 
It was written for somewhere else.

If you’ve taken a product into the Gulf, what caught you out first?

P.S. Mistake number 4 is pricing in USD and calling it localisation 🙃

Dubai brokers, brokerages and developers are now playing a massive game of catch up with AI.

But the problem is everyone’s busy and there’s no proper guidance on how to set it up properly.

Here’s what happens…

Brokers:

Brokers are logging in, giving basic promos like “produce a sales offer” and then getting frustrated when the template / layout is poor and when loads of information is wrong or not as expected.

So a few weeks spending time on this goes by, getting maybe 30-40% of the way there (if that). Eventually giving up when it’s taking longer to do with AI, than without.

Brokerages / Developers:

For real estate agencies, it’s implemented within management, but again, pretty generic.

No true “voice” or set up vision. Not even a proper idea on what they want AI to do.

Just “automation”. But automate what exactly?

Then, agents who are given free reign to experiment and showing a million different layouts, many which don’t follow the brand.

And finally the risks of inaccurate information, client data security and reputation damage for buyers and sellers seeing poorly set out AI work and starting to question whether this is the company they want to work for.

All the while spending endless time,
Money and resource blindly stabbing at how to to it.

Even with experts in AI, the gap is usually having people implement this that don’t understand this industry.

Especially with off plan automation.

The next 6 months, I see a lot of agents and companies trying to rewind
cards.why: Good peer vendor overview of real estate AI failures. Perfect fit for pushback on deterministic code vs prompts.

options.text: Giving brokers a blank prompt box for sales offers is always going to produce bad layouts and wrong facts. If it touches pricing, code needs to fetch the data first.

If a clinic model works only when its founder is in the room, it is not a model.

That is the second test I would set before scaling anything in Saudi Arabia.

Test 2: can a licensed local team deliver it reliably? Not once. Not with your best people.

Every day, with the team you can actually hire. A model is real only when: 

1. A new hire can follow it in the first week without asking the founder.
2. Two different clinicians, on two different days, deliver the same standard.
3. The handoffs are written down: reception to clinician, clinician to follow-up, follow-up to patient.
4. Every step has an owner, by role.

The expansion problems I worry about most are operational, not clinical.
So here is the check I would run.

Step away for two weeks.

If quality, scheduling and patient communication hold, you have a model.
If they do not, you have a dependency.

To those building clinics and hospitals in the Kingdom: what breaks first when a model moves to a new market: staffing, scheduling or patient communication?

options.text: Patient communication almost always breaks first. When you step away, do those reception-to-follow-up handoffs tend to stay in WhatsApp or is there a system holding them?

Having handoffs written down is a good start, but if they rely on manual updates in WhatsApp, they fall apart the moment you step away. Ownership by role only holds up when the system automatically routes the next step to the right person without anyone having to chase it.

cards.author_headline: CSO · Advisor & Builder in Personalised Medicine & AI 🇸🇦 🇫🇷
cards.post_text:
Longevity in Saudi Arabia does not mean what it means in the US, France or Japan, and that is not a detail. 

In Los Angeles, longevity is often a performance project. You track your sleep scores, your biological age, you pay cash to become a better version of himself.

In Paris, longevity is often a prevention conversation. It happens late, inside a system that reimburses illness. 

In Tokyo, longevity is a societal question. Nearly three in ten people are over 65. The goal is autonomy, dignity, staying useful to your community for as long as possible.

In Riyadh, longevity answers a different question entirely. 

Most of the population is under 35. The customer is young, already exposed to diabetes, weight gain and sedentary work. The reference point is not the biological clock, it is how you look, how you perform, and how discreetly you can take care of both.

Same word, different patients, payers, goals, definitions of success.

This is why some longevity concepts imported into the region need more than a translation. 

They often bring a good answer to a different question: anti-ageing promises to people who do not feel old, data dashboards to clients who value intimacy and speed over metrics, long programmes built around slow, incremental change for a clientele that expects visible results quickly. The goals are not the same because the starting points are simply different. 

What people measure themselves against, what they consider healthy, what they expect from care,
cards.why: Deeply insightful post on KSA longevity market differences. Excellent alignment with Riyadh clinic buyers.

options.text: That observation about clients valuing intimacy and speed over metrics is right on the mark. If intake feels like a generic corporate form, Riyadh clients lose interest fast.

The gap between fast client expectations and slow operational backends is real. When I mapped a Saudi medical distributor's workflow serving local clinics, the biggest delays were manual phone calls and admin loops. You can sell a fast, discreet experience upfront, but if the back-office intake takes days, the whole promise falls apart.

Framing Riyadh longevity as look and performance for a younger population hits the core difference. Are you seeing local clinics successfully rebuild their patient intake around quick, private interactions, or are most still trying to import long western intake forms and data dashboards?

cards.post_text:
How to check a Dubai real estate broker in two minutes

Buying in Dubai from abroad means trusting someone you may never meet. The good news: you can check that person in about two minutes.

1. Ask for the BRN

Every broker in Dubai must hold a Broker Registration Number issued by RERA. Look it up in the Dubai REST app or on the Dubai Land Department website. The name and the brokerage should match. Mine is BRN 62633, and I'm happy when clients check it.

2. Ask for DLD data, not opinions

A good broker shows you registered DLD transactions for the same building and layout. "The market price is X" isn't data. "Here are the last five deals for this layout, with floors and dates" is.

3. Insist on the official forms

Form A is the agreement between seller and broker. Form B is between buyer and broker. Form F is the MOU between buyer and seller. If someone wants a deposit before Form F is signed, walk away.

4. Get the total cost in writing

DLD 4%, agency commission, trustee fees, developer fees on off-plan. A broker who can't put this on one page before you commit isn't ready to handle your money.

5. Check the track record

Platform status (for example Property Finder SuperAgent), references and real cases with numbers.

Red flags I'd never ignore:
- pressure to pay before an MOU
- a price far below every recent DLD deal, with no explanation
- reluctance to share the BRN

It takes two minutes and it saves a lot of money.

Full guide: https://lnkd.in/dxSaf9g6

#DubaiRealEstat
cards.why: Dubai broker sharing practical buyer advice.

options.text: Insisting on Form F before any deposit changes everything for someone buying from abroad. That one rule saves so much headache.
Getting the total cost on one page upfront is rare. When the DLD 4%, trustee fees, and developer charges all land on a single sheet, you immediately know who actually knows the numbers.
Asking for DLD data instead of opinions is the right filter. Do most international buyers actually check those past five deals themselves, or do they rely on the broker to pull them?

cards.author_headline: A Great Property Can Still Be a Terrible Investment. || I Challenge the Deal Before You Commit the Capital || Real Estate Broker + Litigator ||
cards.post_text:
Your Airbnb pro forma is lying to you.

Not on purpose. But it is.

What happened with my client

Mark*, a Texas landlord with several US rentals, so he's not a beginner.

He sent me a Dubai Marina deal. 
The sheet showed a double-digit yield as an Airbnb. 

He was ready to wire the deposit.
We underwrote it like a deal back home.

Why the usual thinking fails

• Gross is not NOI. Management fees run 15–25%. 
Add cleaning, furniture, utilities, platform fees, permits and service charges 

• The sheet assumed 80%+ occupancy all year. 
Dubai hotels averaged 80.6% in H1 2025, per Dubai's tourism department. 
One unit won't beat the hotels every month.

• Demand is real. Dubai drew 19.59M overnight visitors in 2025. 
So is supply. Dubai Land Department logged 132,500 off-plan sales in 2025. 
More units. More rivals for your guests.

• STRs need a holiday home permit. 
Some buildings ban them. 
Think of an HOA that bans rentals under 30 days.

• US tax still applies. Think IRS, FBAR and FATCA.
My 9 years in law helped here. 
Mark's building had rules the brochure left out.

The outcome

We did not kill the deal. We fixed it. 
Real occupancy. Clean title. SPA checked line by line. 

A long-term lease as plan B. 
He bought a better unit and closed with confidence.

My independent view

• Underwrite the long-term lease. STR income is upside.
• Stress-test occupancy 20–30% below the brochure.
• Check permits and building rules first.
• Get your contract reviewed by someone on your sid
cards.why: Real estate investment due diligence post by an expert; good context on market reality but limited AI angle.

options.text: Treating long-term lease as the baseline and STR as upside changes the whole math. How often do buyers actually run that comparison before putting down a deposit?
That 15-25% management fee line usually catches overseas buyers off guard. Once you add utilities, building rules, and platform cuts, that double-digit pro forma yield shrinks in a hurry.

Stress-testing occupancy 20 to 30 percent below the brochure makes sense, especially with 132,500 off-plan units hitting the market. When you run that test for clients, how many of these Marina deals actually survive on long-term rental income alone?

Here is the part most people skip.

You can inspect the building, read the service charge, walk the neighborhood at 8 pm, and buy something you will still want in ten years.

That is a very different market from the one we had in 2024, when people bought off a floor p

For a patient who traveled for his hair transplant, the care stops at the airport.

He flies home on day 2. To Berlin, Riyadh, Sao Paulo. From that moment, the clinic that operated on him is in another country, on another clock, and often in another language.

Then day 8 comes, with its question in front of the mirror. He writes at 23:12. Nobody answers that night.

I say this to surgeons and it makes them uncomfortable, so I will say it here too: a clinic that operates on patients from abroad and goes silent once they land sells an operation, not a result.

The medicine can be excellent. I have seen it be excellent. The patient will remember the week nobody answered.

Calling out the clinic that goes silent once the patient lands is a fair point. When you talk to these clinic teams, is the main bottleneck usually coverage across time zones, or handling multi-language questions past clinic hours?

cards.author_headline: Co-Founder
cards.post_text:
That quote from the Turkish dental clinic looks cheap. It probably isn't.

A proper dental quote should list each procedure separately, crown, extraction, X-ray, consultation, with a price against every single line. If you get one number with no breakdown, that's not a quote. That's a figure designed to get you on a plane.

"All-inclusive" is the phrase to watch. It usually covers the treatment itself and sometimes a hotel transfer. It rarely covers follow-up appointments, remedial work if something goes wrong, the consultation before treatment starts, or flights home if you need an emergency return. Those gaps can cost more than the original saving.

Before you commit, ask the clinic these three questions: What happens if I need additional work once treatment starts? Is aftercare included if I have complications back in the UK? What is your complaint and redress process? A good clinic will answer all three in writing without hesitation. An evasive response tells you something important.

Always get two quotes and lay them side by side. Not just the total, the line items. A quote missing sedation costs, temporary fittings, or a post-treatment check is artificially low. You're not comparing the same thing.

One thing worth checking: does the clinic hold any recognised accreditation? JCI accreditation is one of the more rigorous international standards for hospitals and clinics. It doesn't guarantee a perfect outcome, but it means someone external has checked their processes.
cards.why: Co-founder breaking down medical tourism quotes and transparent patient communication. Matches dental story nicely.

options.text: That line about getting answers 'in writing without hesitation' is huge. When patients ask about aftercare, do most clinics have a set policy ready or is it usually vague until pushed?

Calling out how 'all-inclusive' quotes hide temporary fittings and post-treatment checks hits the real issue. A single package price makes it impossible to tell if follow-up care is included once you return home.

I'd almost rank clear written aftercare terms higher than JCI accreditation for someone traveling abroad. An international standard shows their clinic facility was audited, but written agreement on who pays for local remedial work is what actually protects the patient.

cards.author_headline: CEO and Founder
cards.post_text:
Being an excellent dentist does not make you a good practice owner.

A clinic is a company. It has accounting, finance, marketing, HR, contracts, operations and real estate. Clinical skill is one part of the equation, not the whole of it.

I am starting a series on building a dental practice in Saudi Arabia, using Riyadh as the example because it is the hardest market to get right: high competition, rents that rose sharply in recent years, informed patients who compare, and high expectations for the environment and experience.

The first decision is not location. It is whether you are ready.

For most new graduates, the honest answer is: work first. The most expensive lessons are better learned on someone else's balance sheet. Government roles build clinical depth. Private hospitals expose you to systems, quality and insurance. A mid-sized private clinic shows you the business up close: why patients do not return, why chairs sit empty at 4 pm and overflow at 8 pm, why the best clinician is not always the highest earner.

Signs you are ready:
- Patients who follow you by name
- A clear idea of what you will offer, and to whom
- Capital that covers setup plus several months of operating losses
- People you trust in finance and administration
- Patience

Signs you are not:
- Opening because a colleague did
- Projecting revenue but not costs
- Not knowing the difference between profit and cash

Then come the structural choices: start from scratch or acquire, go alone or partner.
cards.why: Saudi dental practice founder discussing operational realities and empty chairs.

options.text: That line about chairs sitting empty at 4 PM while 8 PM overflows is so real for Riyadh. Is the afternoon slump usually patient preference, or just how front desks handle scheduling?

Learning why patients don't return on someone else's balance sheet is spot on. A lot of those empty 4 PM slots happen simply because an enquiry came in after hours and sat in a WhatsApp inbox until the next morning.

Having patients follow you by name is great for starting out, but it can be a double-edged sword. If the chair count depends entirely on personal doctor loyalty rather than clinic intake systems, keeping those 4 PM slots filled gets tough the moment you expand.

If an algorithm slashes peak-season ADR by 70% in the GCC. How your Asset Management team safeguarded you.
​When autonomous pricing, central distribution, or AI Agents fail, operators are pointing to third-party tech dependencies to seek liability relief or excuse underperformance.

​Are these policies available in the GCC?
Yes. While mainland domestic policies often miss the mark, specialized AI & Tech Errors & Omissions (E&O) and System Failure Business Interruption coverages are being structured via the DIFC, ADGM, and international reinsurance syndicates.
​To protect assets against this gap, GCC Hotel Management Agreements (HMAs) must anchor four non-negotiable protections:
​Explicit FM Carve-Outs: Strictly bar algorithmic errors and SaaS failures from excusing operator performance.
​Specialized AI & Tech E&O Mandates: Require operators and vendors to carry AI-inclusive Tech E&O and Cyber coverages via DIFC/ADGM or international syndicates to cover the financial fallout of algorithmic errors.
​Protected Performance Tests: Prevent automated distribution missteps from being excluded from RevPAR Index or GOP covenant tests.
​Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Controls: Require 24/7 m
cards.why: Hospitality asset management discussing algorithmic liability and guardrails. Aligns well with opinions on deterministic code over prompts.

options.text: Relying on contractual policy for rate floors usually fails. If the floor is hardcoded into the execution logic, the algorithm physically can't drop the price past it.

That 70% ADR drop scenario usually happens when the model has direct write access. In an inventory system I built, I made the AI read-and-propose only. The actual commit is handled by rule-based code, so the system literally rejects any price change below the preset floor regardless of what the AI suggests.

Requiring 24/7 manual overrides in an HMA sounds right on paper, but can an asset team realistically catch a rogue repricing run at 2 AM before central distribution syncs it? If the floor isn't enforced programmatically at the API layer, human-in-the-loop usually just means writing the incident report after the damage is done.

I am a commercial broker in Dubai and i have worked with several business owners who were looking for a new commercial space or planning expansion.

Parts of Dubai are recovering, and some are performing exceptionally well. Residential RE in major areas have contracted quite a bit, unless you are a business owner or in revenue generating role, commercial has also taken a quite a hit.

Surviving businesses report stronger orders. Finance and healthcare are expanding. Schools have started, local aviation capacity has largely returned, the population is at a record, and the best property still attracts buyers.

At the same time, fewer new businesses are being formed and a large number of existing licences have gone quiet. New tenants are paying materially less than a year ago while sitting tenants are being asked to pay more. The risk to rent is rarely the average. It is the marginal business, the marginal job, the next household, the leveraged owner and the next apartment that needs a tenant.

Compared to 2025, there has been a fall in number of active licensees being formed and increasing number of licenses not being renewed which in direct has affected employment. Most displaced jobs sit in trading, site trades, hospitality, retail, F&B, real estate and transport.

Over summer, central bank introduced number of financial packages in the form of deferred installments, and waiving of credit. Temporary relief can postpone the moment a weak borrower becomes visible in delinquency

options.text: You called AI the final boss for commercial tenants. Are you seeing brokers deal with clients shrinking space due to AI headcount cuts, or is it just cash preservation?

That gap between sitting tenants paying more while new ones pay less is sharp. In operational workflows, when margin pressure hits, companies usually freeze new software spend and external hires long before they give up physical floor space.

I doubt AI is the reason commercial footprints are shrinking just yet. Most GCC businesses adopting AI right now use it to handle extra workload without adding headcount, not to lay off whole teams and vacate floors.

cards.author_headline: CEO, Googan Business Services | Ph.D. in Strategy | Feasibility Studies, Market Research & Investment Advisory for Saudi Arabia since 1996 | دراسات الجدوى | دراسة السوق | Riyadh
cards.post_text:
The towers arrive before the residents.

In Riyadh's newer districts, the roads, the streetlights and the first buildings are often in place long before the people who will live there. For anyone opening a shop, a clinic or a café in that district, the gap between "built" and "lived in" is the real risk.

I have seen good concepts open on the right street, in the right district, two years too early. The location was not wrong. The timing was.

Before signing a lease in a district that is still filling up, I ask three questions:

1. How many units around the site are occupied today, not planned?
2. At what pace are new residents actually moving in?
3. How many months of fixed costs can the business carry while the catchment fills?

The answer usually changes the lease more than the concept: a shorter first term, a rent-free fit-out period, or a smaller first unit.

Growth on the map and customers at the door arrive on different dates. Plan for both.

#Riyadh #RealEstate #FeasibilityStudy #SaudiArabia
cards.why: Feasibility study expert discussing clinic timing and occupancy in new Riyadh districts.

options.text: That gap between built and lived in hits new clinics hard here in Riyadh. How often do you see owners actually negotiate a rent-free fit-out period long enough?

The gap between built and lived in shows up across the whole supply chain in Riyadh. When I mapped a distributor's workflow delivering to 50-60 clinics and pharmacies, routes into newly built districts ran at low volume for months while residential move-ins lagged behind. Getting that rent-free fit-out period right is huge.

Taking a smaller first unit makes sense on paper, but for medical clinics it can backfire. If the layout is too tight to add services or equipment later, you end up paying for a full refit or moving right as the neighborhood finally fills up. Do you usually see clinics successfully expand in place?

A question for anyone opening a shop, clinic or café in Riyadh:

Would you take the prime location with high rent, or a secondary location with the difference spent on marketing?

The prime site buys visibility every day without asking. The secondary site keeps fixed costs lower and puts the money into reaching customers directly. Both can work, and both can fail.

My view: it depends on how your customers arrive. If they buy on impulse, while passing by, the location is the marketing and the rent is worth it. If they plan the visit and search before they go, a good secondary site with easy parking and strong visibility online often wins.

Which did you choose, and would you choose it again?

options.text: For a clinic on a secondary site, putting that extra rent money into ads only works if the front desk actually picks up when those calls come in.

When I needed a dentist at 11 PM, I called 5 clinics: 3 didn't pick up, 1 had a robotic hours message, and 1 had an Arabic-only voicemail. The 6th clinic answered, got the appointment and won the patient.

I'd push back on a secondary site winning just because customers search before they go. When a patient searches online, they usually message two or three clinics at once. If the front desk takes hours to reply on WhatsApp, that ad spend just paid for the competitor's appointment.

Anyone in real estate sales knows what a closed deal takes: weeks of calls and follow-ups, securing the right units, rounds of negotiation, and the stress that comes with all of it.

Yet in some corners of our market, giving up a large share of your hard-earned commission has become normal. Some salespeople hand back as much as 50% just to get a deal over the line, even when working directly with a developer.

It started as a shortcut. It has become a habit, and it is time to end it.

Beyond what it does to your income, kickbacks carry real risk. Brokers in the UAE are regulated under the country’s anti-money laundering framework, and undisclosed or unusual payments can raise serious compliance questions for everyone involved. A transparent, documented commission arrangement is the only safe way to do business.

So here is my message to my fellow professionals:

Your work has value. Your commission is earned, not negotiable. And a deal that depends on you giving up half your payout is not a good deal.

Let’s raise the standard together: full payouts, clear agreements, and honest business.

#DubaiRealEstate #RealEstateSales #SalesProfessionals #ProfessionalEthics #UAEProperty #SalesCommission #SalesIncentives #FairPay #EthicalSelling #BusinessEthics #Compliance #OffPlanDubai #DubaiInvestment

options.text: Giving up 50% of a commission just to close usually comes from desperation. Are buyers demanding kickbacks here, or are agents undercutting each other on the same developer units?

Spending weeks on calls only to give up half the commission usually means the pipeline is leaking at the front end. When half your incoming enquiries go cold before anyone answers, every deal feels like a life-or-death negotiation. Fixing that waste at intake gives agents the backing to stand firm on their full payout.

The compliance risk around anti-money laundering is real, Sunil, but telling individual agents to stand firm won't change much while rival brokerages quietly look the other way. Until developers strictly audit where buyer rebates are coming from, honest agents who refuse to give up 50% will just keep losing clients to someone who will.

17 years in healthcare finance. Five lessons I wish I'd learned earlier.

3) A reconciliation nobody reviews is just a spreadsheet.

4) The best finance decisions are made with operations in the room, not about them.

5) Systems change every few years. Discipline in the monthly close doesn't.

Healthcare finance isn't just reporting. It's keeping good medicine sustainable.

A clinic in Dubai loses more money to missed appointments than to any marketing problem.

It is not a Dubai-only problem, but Dubai makes it expensive: rent is high, every empty slot costs, and the patient who forgot will book somewhere else next time.

Here is the WhatsApp booking flow I would ship for a clinic in two weeks, in the order it earns its money back:

1. Booking in two taps. The patient picks a doctor and a slot inside WhatsApp. No app to download, no form to fill.

2. Confirmation with a token number, instantly. A token number feels real. "We will call you back" does not.

3. Reminder 24 hours before, and again 2 hours before, with Confirm and Reschedule buttons. This is the step that cuts no-shows the most.

4. Follow-up the next day: "How are you feeling? Reply 1 to book a review." Repeat visits without a receptionist making calls.

5. A daily report to the owner at 9 pm: bookings, no-shows, revenue at risk. On WhatsApp, not in a dashboard nobody opens.

Everything runs on the clinic's own WhatsApp Business number. The number, the data and the patient list stay with the clinic, not with us.

Cost: a fixed price in writing, before work starts. Time: two weeks. Languages: English, Hindi and Urdu, with Arabic message templates on request.

If you run a clinic, a salon or any appointment business in the UAE or Saudi Arabia and want to see this on your own phone, message me. The first 15 minutes are free.

#Dubai #Healthcare #WhatsAppBusiness #SmallBusiness #GCC
cards.why: Peer outlining clinic WhatsApp booking flows. Good angle to push deterministic backend logic.

options.text: That reminder flow works great when people actually tap the buttons, but what happens when a patient replies with a raw text message like actually can I come at 4 instead? That is where the chat logic usually breaks down.
How does the 9 pm WhatsApp report handle it when a patient cancels right before closing? Does it flag that for the front desk first thing in the morning?

When frontline teams and physicians sit at the same table, the patient’s experience becomes clearer.

I started holding patient services and physicians engagement meetings after noticing something familiar: physicians would sometimes raise concerns that frontline teams were not following booking policy or were accepting patients inconsistently.

From the frontline team side, the situation often looked different, as they were dealing with real-time constraints, patient needs, and operational pressures that physicians may not see from the clinic side.

So I brought both groups together.

The purpose was simple: make sure we share the same intention, put the 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁, and communicate one clear message across physicians and the frontline teams, including OPD reception, allied health reception, and the call center.

When physicians and frontline staff discuss the same issue together, each side sees the full picture. Reception & Call Center understands the clinical expectations and Physicians understand the operational realities, then both sides can agree on what “best service” should look like for the patient.

What has stood out to me is how well the both teams respond to these meetings. People take ownership because they believe patient experience is everyone’s responsibility, not the responsibility of one department.

We’ve recently implemented AI solutions in few independent dental practices. And honestly, not all of them worked, at first attempt.

Over time, we’ve worked on implementing AI-driven solutions for independent dental practices, focusing on areas such as lead management, patient communication, appointment scheduling, and operational efficiency. (Basically all the areas directly connected with Revenue).

Some implementations delivered meaningful improvements.

Others didn’t produce the results we expected.

And a few simply failed.

Here’s what we learned:

1. AI doesn’t fix a broken workflow.

Automating an inefficient process only makes inefficiency happen faster. Before introducing AI, you need to understand how the practice actually operates.

2. Technology isn’t always the problem.

Sometimes the issue is staff adoption. Sometimes it’s poor data. Sometimes it’s an existing process that nobody wants to change.

3. More automation doesn’t necessarily mean better results.

A dental practice doesn’t need another AI tool. It needs solutions that help convert more inquiries into appointments, reduce missed opportunities, and improve the patient experience.

4. Every clinic is different.

What works in one practice might fail in another. Patient demographics, team structure, existing software, and internal processes all matter.

Our biggest takeaway?

Implementing AI is not about deploying agents, connecting APIs, or building impressive dashboards.

It’s about understanding a bus

Dubai gained 226,885 residents between January and late September 2026, according to the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment.

Many of them will choose a GP, dentist, or paediatrician here for the first time. For clinics, that is a steady flow of new patients.

It can also hide a leak.

In a growing city, new-patient numbers can rise while a clinic quietly loses the patients it has already won. The dashboard looks healthy, but the patient base never compounds.

In Dubai, market retention is a growth strategy, not an admin task. It rests on four habits:

1. Clear next step: before patients leave, they know what follow-up their doctor advised and how to book it.
2. Easy rebooking: a follow-up is as easy to book as the first visit, with no details re-entered.
3. Opt-in reminders: messages only to patients who have consented, with no clinical detail. UAE PDPL, the federal health data law, and DHA advertising standards all apply.
4. Measure returns: track repeat visits next to new patients, not instead of them.

None of this needs a big budget. It needs an owner and a system that remembers.

A question for Dubai clinic leaders: of the new patients you saw last quarter, do you know how many came back?

This happened to me yesterday...

I asked a developer’s sales agent for help with a client. The deal was already done, and suddenly nobody wanted to know.

Here is what happened:

→ The developer is late handing over the property.
→ I asked when clients will receive their handover notices. The answer: “Email customer care.”
→ I asked for an approximate date. The answer: “Email customer care.”

The UAE is becoming more than a business destination. It is becoming a place where people build businesses, establish their families, and invest for the future.

Where is the real opportunity in the UAE property market today?

But what makes this interesting is the difference between property types:

🏢 Apartments: Approximately 12% annual price growth
🏡 Villas & Townhouses: Approximately 15% annual price growth

Source: Cushman & Wakefield Core, Dubai Residential Market Update 2025.

This comparison highlights an important investment lesson:

Not every property performs the same way, even within the same city.

Location, property type, supply, connectivity, community infrastructure, and buyer demand can all influence appreciation.

📈 What about Dubai's market growth?

Dubai's residential property prices increased:

• 22% in 2023
• 18% in 2024
• 13% in 2025

The market continued to grow, but the rate of appreciation moderated.

This is why I believe investors should focus on more than just the previous year's growth.

The better questions are:

✔ Is the location supported by real infrastructure development?
✔ Is there genuine demand

cards.author_headline: Founder & CEO ADONIS Medical Group | Founder A.EggBank & Vitality Biotech | MD | IVF & Reproductive Tech | Global Egg Donor Bank | Life Sciences Investor | 25y Healthcare
cards.post_text:
Should a good doctor understand the economics of medicine? 💬

I think so. Resources are always limited: a doctor's time, equipment, the work of the team, the patient's money. Clinical decisions have economic consequences, even when we don't talk about them.

Knowing the cost of an examination, understanding how busy a room is, or following the financial results of your own department is normal. It helps a doctor see beyond a single appointment and use resources more responsibly.

There is a clear line: the profitability of a procedure cannot be a reason to prescribe it. If a patient doesn't need an examination, a free machine or an unmet financial plan doesn't make it necessary.

Responsibility also lies with owners and management. We cannot demand well-grounded prescriptions from a doctor and then judge them only by how much money they brought in. The incentive system has to match the principles we declare.

A doctor should understand how the clinic earns, and the patient should be sure that a prescription was made because they need it. Combining these two is the job of leadership.

How do you keep incentives in line with the principles your clinic declares?

#healthcareleadership #healthcaremanagement #medicalethics #healthcareeconomics #ADONIS
cards.why: Medical group CEO discussing clinic economics and resource allocation.

options.text: Measuring a doctor by how much money they brought in almost guarantees clinical decisions get compromised. Vitaliy, do your department heads track administrative hours lost alongside room utilization?

When I mapped a distributor's workflow supplying 50+ clinics, the biggest resource leak wasn't equipment downtime: it was staff placing 20 to 30 internal calls every time an item went out of stock. When basic coordination eats up that much time, judging doctors on revenue misses where the actual operational cost lives.

Expecting doctors to keep department financial results in mind while treating patients feels like a risky overlap. If the goal is grounded prescriptions, shouldn't doctors focus purely on patient care while leadership manages room utilization in the background?

Weeks of work. An AED 20 million deal. Lost.

Even after years in real estate, losing a deal like that still hurts.

My wife noticed it immediately. I usually need about 24 hours to process the disappointment.

But she offered a different perspective:
"Maybe that deal wasn't meant for you. Maybe you were being protected from something you couldn't see."

Initially, I struggled to see it that way.

Then I watched how things unfolded. The buyer walked away, forfeited his deposit and decided he wouldn't be returning to Dubai or Abu Dhabi. The agent who expected to close the transaction lost it too.

It reinforced an important lesson about business:
Not every opportunity is a good opportunity, and not every lost deal is a failure.

Sometimes we become so focused on securing the transaction that we forget to consider what might happen after the signature.

Experience isn't just about learning how to win deals. It's also about recognising when walking away, or losing an opportunity, might be the better outcome.

💬 What's the biggest deal you've ever lost, and how did things turn out in the end?

🎥 We discuss this in the latest full episode on YouTube. Link in bio.
